questions.article: The Price of Being a Taker
questions.q: In Chicago in 1893 a woman judged Swami Vivekananda by his simple dress. What did he tell her?
options: That where he came from, character, not the tailor, makes a gentleman
Yes. Politely said.
That his clothes were costly at home
Not quite. The article says: That where he came from, character, not the tailor, makes a gentleman.
That she had no right to comment
Not quite. The article says: That where he came from, character, not the tailor, makes a gentleman.
That he would dress differently next time
Not quite. The article says: That where he came from, character, not the tailor, makes a gentleman.
questions.rationale: “In your country it is the tailor who makes a man a gentleman, but in the country from which I come, it is character which makes a man a gentleman.”

questions.q: The article asks us to think about a car beyond the money paid for it. What does such reflection reveal?
options: That inventors were mostly lucky
Not quite. The article says: It is God’s gift in potential, made real by the labour of countless people – so we owe gratitude to God and to humanity.
That cars are a needless luxury
Not quite. The article says: It is God’s gift in potential, made real by the labour of countless people – so we owe gratitude to God and to humanity.
That the buyer alone deserves credit
Not quite. The article says: It is God’s gift in potential, made real by the labour of countless people – so we owe gratitude to God and to humanity.
It is God’s gift in potential, made real by the labour of countless people – so we owe gratitude to God and to humanity
Well reasoned. This is the root of the “love-all” outlook.
questions.rationale: “Modern vehicles are God-given, in terms of potential. And since many countries and their citizens were involved in turning this natural potential into actual, these vehicles are also a gift from humanity.”

questions.q: What did the Prophet say of one who does not acknowledge people?
options: He will be acknowledged by no one
Not quite. The article says: He cannot acknowledge God either.
He needs more education
Not quite. The article says: He cannot acknowledge God either.
He cannot acknowledge God either
Right. Gratitude is not divisible.
He should be left alone
Not quite. The article says: He cannot acknowledge God either.
questions.rationale: “One who does not acknowledge people, cannot even acknowledge God.”

questions.q: Shackleton’s men survived months stranded on drifting ice. What, according to the book quoted, lay beneath their optimism?
options: The confidence that their situation was only temporary
Yes. No difficulty lasts forever.
A large store of supplies
Not quite. The article says: The confidence that their situation was only temporary.
Regular contact with home
Not quite. The article says: The confidence that their situation was only temporary.
Their leader’s strict discipline
Not quite. The article says: The confidence that their situation was only temporary.
questions.rationale: “Underlying the optimism of the party was the confidence that their situation was only temporary.”

questions.q: What does the article call the positive gain of old age?
options: Freedom from all duties
Not quite. The article says: The discovery of one’s helplessness, which leads to humility and to God – with wisdom to share.
The respect that age commands
Not quite. The article says: The discovery of one’s helplessness, which leads to humility and to God – with wisdom to share.
The discovery of one’s helplessness, which leads to humility and to God – with wisdom to share
Well read. Hence “the golden age.”
More time for rest
Not quite. The article says: The discovery of one’s helplessness, which leads to humility and to God – with wisdom to share.
questions.rationale: “Old age has a positive aspect to it—a gain that only results with agedness—and that is the discovery of one’s helplessness.”

questions.q: By what familiar example does the article explain “conviction without observation”?
options: We believe in the wind though it is unseen
Not quite. The article says: Everyone is certain who his mother is, though no one witnessed his own birth.
We trust maps of places we have not visited
Not quite. The article says: Everyone is certain who his mother is, though no one witnessed his own birth.
Everyone is certain who his mother is, though no one witnessed his own birth
Right. Certainty need not rest on sight.
We remember dreams we cannot prove
Not quite. The article says: Everyone is certain who his mother is, though no one witnessed his own birth.
questions.rationale: “Everyone has complete conviction in one’s mother despite not having witnessed or observed one’s birth from her womb.”

questions.article: A Believer’s Attitude Towards His Neighbour
questions.q: “He is not a believer who eats to his fill while his neighbour goes without food.” What does the article say this teaching shows?
options: Neighbours should eat together daily
Not quite. The article says: A believer cares about others’ hunger as about his own, and gives practical help.
A believer cares about others’ hunger as about his own, and gives practical help
Yes. Goodwill alone is not enough.
One should eat very little
Not quite. The article says: A believer cares about others’ hunger as about his own, and gives practical help.
Charity is owed only to relatives
Not quite. The article says: A believer cares about others’ hunger as about his own, and gives practical help.
questions.rationale: “This shows that a Muslim is one who is concerned with others’ hunger and thirst as he is with his own.”

questions.article: A Believer’s Attitude Towards His Neighbour
questions.q: According to the article, a faithful servant of God lives in one of two ways. Which?
options: As a teacher or a student
Not quite. The article says: As a giver, or at least as a no-problem person.
As a giver, or at least as a no-problem person
Correct. “There is no third option.”
As a host or a guest
Not quite. The article says: As a giver, or at least as a no-problem person.
As a leader or a follower
Not quite. The article says: As a giver, or at least as a no-problem person.
questions.rationale: “For a man to be a really faithful servant of God, he must live either as a giver or as a no-problem person. There is no third option.”

questions.q: Why, in the article’s analysis, do some people prefer money to relationships?
options: Money brings more respect
Not quite. The article says: Money asks nothing in return, whereas people require give and take.
People are harder to find than money
Not quite. The article says: Money asks nothing in return, whereas people require give and take.
Money asks nothing in return, whereas people require give and take
Well reasoned. But the choice is unnatural and leaves one divided.
Money lasts longer than friendship
Not quite. The article says: Money asks nothing in return, whereas people require give and take.
questions.rationale: “With money, you can make contact on unilateral basis, but with human beings, you have to make contact on a bilateral basis, that is, on a give and take basis.”

questions.q: A train reaches its destination only while it stays on its rails. What does the article say takes a person “off the rails”?
options: Travelling too slowly
Not quite. The article says: Becoming absorbed in something other than God – selfish desire, hatred, or devotion to a person or party.
Asking others for directions
Not quite. The article says: Becoming absorbed in something other than God – selfish desire, hatred, or devotion to a person or party.
Becoming absorbed in something other than God – selfish desire, hatred, or devotion to a person or party
Exactly. Any such detour misses the goal.
Stopping to rest on the way
Not quite. The article says: Becoming absorbed in something other than God – selfish desire, hatred, or devotion to a person or party.
questions.rationale: “One tends to stray from the straight path whenever one is obsessed with something, person or idea, other than God.”
